subject: mathematics
question_text: By the Gauss-Jordan method, solve x + y + z = 9, 2x + 5y + 7z = 52, 2x + y − z = 0.

mark_split.label: Clear column 1 below the leading entry
Reach a leading 1 in the last row

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.51, chapter 5 MATRICES, Long Answer question 9(ii), Gauss-Jordan route. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+2+1+3+1 split weights the row reduction — two marks for clearing down and three for clearing up — against the setup and the finish, and matches every other unique-solution Gauss-Jordan answer in this unit. ONE CARD PER METHOD: the book asks this one system by matrix inversion, by Cramer's rule and by the Gauss-Jordan method, and this bank answers each method on its own card so that a student who opens one never has to read another. The siblings are ts_ipe_m1a_mat_cramer_x_y_z_9_2x5y7z52 and ts_ipe_m1a_mat_inverse_x_y_z_9_2x5y7z52, and all three land on the same solution x = 1, y = 3, z = 5. Working checked twice: Δ = det A was expanded along R₁ and again along C₁, both giving −4, so the system was known to have one solution before the row reduction started, and the solution was substituted back into all three original equations (9 = 9, 52 = 52, 0 = 0). Paper position: Maths-1A Section C prints 3 long answers at 8 marks each and the student answers any 2; Matrices is one of the units that can fill a Section-C slot. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this by the Gauss-Jordan method — say what matrix you write down first, which direction you clear in, and how you check the answer.

steps.label: Write the augmented matrix
steps.margin_note: First mark. The augmented matrix is A with the constants column joined on. The rule down the middle is not decoration — it marks where the equals sign was, and every row operation acts across it.
steps.memory_tip: The augmented matrix is A with the constants column joined on; the rule marks where the equals sign was.
lines: The system in matrix form is AX = D, where

lines.text: A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & 7 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \ X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \ D = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 52 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That the augmented matrix [A | D] is written — the coefficient matrix with the constants column attached.
accept: write the augmented matrix A D with the constants joined on to the coefficient matrix
form A given D by putting the right hand side as a fourth column
write the coefficient matrix together with the constants column
augmented matrix rasta, coefficients tho patu constants column kuda
attach the constants to A to make the augmented matrix

steps.why: Every row of the augmented matrix IS one of the original equations. That is why a row operation is legal — adding one equation to another never changes the solution set.
common_mistakes: Writing A alone and doing the row operations without the constants.
Putting the constants in as a fourth ROW instead of a fourth column.
Writing the coefficients in the order they appear rather than in x, y, z order.

steps.label: Clear column 1
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The top-left entry is already 1, so clear column 1 straight away. Row 3 then reads −1 in column 2; swapping it up and multiplying by −1 gives a leading 1 there too, which keeps every later step free of fractions.
steps.memory_tip: The top-left entry is already 1. After clearing, swap up the row with −1 in column 2 and multiply it by −1.

recall.must_convey: That a leading 1 is obtained in the top-left position and then used to make the rest of column 1 zero.
accept: get a one in the top left corner then subtract multiples of row one to make the rest of the first column zero
use the leading one to clear column one below it
make the first column zeros under the leading entry using row operations
first column lo leading one techi, kinda unna entries ni zero chestham
swap or subtract to get a one on top then knock out the entries below it

steps.why: Gauss-Jordan works one column at a time, and it always wants a 1 at the pivot first. Chasing zeros before you have that 1 is what forces fractions into the working.
common_mistakes: Clearing the column with a pivot that is not 1, which forces fractions into every later row.
Applying an operation to only part of a row — every entry moves, including the constant.
Changing the pivot row while using it to clear the others.

steps.label: Reach a leading 1 in R₃
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Once row 3 reads 0 0 1 with a number after the rule, z = 5 is already known — everything from here is bookkeeping to get x and y out.
steps.memory_tip: Once row 3 reads 0 0 1, z is known; everything after is bookkeeping for x and y.

recall.must_convey: That the last row is reduced to 0, 0, 1 with the value of z after the rule — that is, the third pivot is made 1.
accept: reduce the last row to zero zero one so that z is read directly
make the third pivot a one by dividing the row
get the bottom row to zero zero one which gives z
last row ni zero zero one ga marchali, appudu z telustundi
divide the bottom row so the pivot becomes one and z is known

steps.why: This is the point where Gauss elimination would stop and back-substitute. Gauss-Jordan carries on and clears upwards too, which is why the answer needs no substitution at all.
common_mistakes: Dividing the row by the wrong entry.
Dividing the coefficients but not the constant after the rule.
Stopping here and calling it the answer; only z is known so far.

steps.label: Clear upwards
steps.margin_note: Three marks. Both pivots are 1 by now, so clearing upwards is pure subtraction with no fractions. Row 3 clears column 3 first, then row 2 clears column 2.
steps.memory_tip: Both pivots are 1 by now, so clearing upwards is pure subtraction. Row 3 first, then row 2.

recall.must_convey: That the elimination is then run upwards — using the lower rows to clear the entries ABOVE the pivots, until only the diagonal is left.
accept: now clear upwards using the bottom row to remove the entries above the pivots
work from the bottom up making the entries above each pivot zero
eliminate above the diagonal so only the pivots are left
ippudu paina unna entries ni kuda zero chestham, kinda nunchi paiki
use row three then row two to clear everything above them

steps.why: Clearing upwards as well as downwards is the ONLY difference between Gauss-Jordan and plain Gauss elimination. It buys you an answer you can read straight off, with no back-substitution.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the triangular form and back-substituting; that is Gauss, not Gauss-Jordan.
Clearing upwards before the pivots are 1, which reintroduces fractions.
Forgetting to carry the operation across the rule into the constant.

steps.label: Read off the solution
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Each row is now a one-letter equation, so the answer is read straight off. Put the three values back into the three original equations before you stop.
steps.memory_tip: Each row is now a one-letter equation, so the answer is read off with no substitution. Then check it in the original equations.
lines: Each row is now a single equation:
Row 1: x = 1,  Row 2: y = 3,  Row 3: z = 5

recall.must_convey: That each row of the reduced matrix reads as one equation, giving x = 1, y = 3, z = 5, and that the values are checked in the original equations.
accept: each row is now one equation so read x y and z straight off
the reduced matrix gives x equals one y equals three z equals five directly with no substitution
read the answers from the last column and then check them
prathi row oke equation kabatti x y z direct ga chadavachu
the three rows give the three unknowns immediately

steps.why: A row reading 0 0 1 | 5 is literally the equation z = 5. Understanding that the matrix never stopped being the equations is what makes the whole method feel less like a recipe, and substituting back is what proves no row operation went wrong.
common_mistakes: Reading the values in the wrong order.
Reading the answer off an earlier matrix instead of the final one.
Stopping without substituting the three values back into all three equations.
